# The Museum of Small Thunder

There is a museum at the edge of a town that no longer exists on any map, and it holds only weather.

Not storms — nothing so grand. Just the small thunder that lives in the back of your throat when you almost say something and don't. The quiet exhale of a cloud that wanted to be a sunset but gave up halfway through. The static electricity of a handshake between two people who haven't seen each other since they were children, and one of them has grown into someone unrecognizable.

The curator is a woman named Voss, or maybe that's just what she calls herself when she bothers to talk at all. She doesn't mind silence. She keeps it in jars, actually — labeled and dated and shelved in alphabetical order. Silence from a Sunday morning. Silence from the three seconds after a car accident. Silence from a couple lying in bed, both awake, neither willing to speak first.

They're worth different prices.

The expensive ones are the silences that used to be noise. A father who told jokes every single day, and then one day was buried, and the joke-shaped hole in the dinner table became its own weather system. Voss keeps that one in a jar she handles with gloves. Not because it's fragile, but because it's warm. Some silences hold heat for decades.

People come to the museum sometimes. They wander the halls and read the labels and nod slowly, as though they already know which jar belongs to them. A teenage boy once stood in front of a jar labeled *Silence from a Kitchen on a Tuesday in November* for forty-five minutes before whispering, "That's mine." Voss nodded. She'd known. She always knows.

She never makes them pay.

The barometer in the lobby doesn't measure pressure. It measures intention. Right now it reads something like *curious, slightly afraid, forgetting something important.* Voss glances at it and goes back to her work.

Her work is this: she collects weather because the world keeps losing it.

Not climate. Not temperature. Not the things they measure at the airport. She collects the *microclimates* — the pockets of atmosphere that form around people and places and moments and then dissolve before anyone notices they were there. The warm spot in the hallway where someone sat and worried about a diagnosis. The cold breeze that passes through a wedding. The barometric pressure of waiting for a phone call.

Every room in the museum has its own climate. The Hall of Almosts is humid and close, the way summer feels before it storms. The Room of Long Ago is dry as paper. The room where she keeps weather from children is always, inexplicably, the exact temperature of a living room on a Saturday morning when there is nowhere to go and nothing to do and everything is gentle.

She catalogs the weather of specific moments, and the catalog reads like poetry if you read it the right way.

*Barometric pressure of a man watching his daughter get on a bus.*
*Wind speed of a woman packing a suitcase at 3 a.m.*
*Humidity of two friends laughing so hard they can't breathe.*
*Temperature of a hand on a back.*

She has a shelf she hasn't opened in years. It holds the weather from the last conversation she had with someone she loved, and she keeps it sealed because the label only says *storm* and she is not ready to remember what kind.

There is a room at the very end of the museum that nobody is allowed to enter. It has a sign that reads: *This room contains all the weather that has not happened yet.* Voss opens the door sometimes, just to check, and every time she looks inside she sees something different. Once it was warm and golden and smelled like bread. Once it was the color of someone running toward her. Once it was so still she held her breath.

She does not know what it means.

She has stopped trying to figure it out.

She simply keeps the door slightly open and goes about her work, collecting the small thunder, cataloging the breath of storms too small to name, making a quiet archive of all the feelings that never made it to language.

Outside, the town that no longer exists is somehow still there. The streetlights come on at dusk. Dogs bark at postmen who never arrive. A breeze moves through the trees and carries with it the faint, warm sound of someone somewhere almost laughing.

Voss hears it and writes it down.

She writes it all down.

---

*I could have written the small thunder and ended it there. But the jars keep calling, and the shelves are long, and somewhere in the back of your throat there's a sound you almost made — and I am here to keep it safe.*
